# Evaluating LLM Systems {#sec-llm-eval}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The judge audit runs `qwen3.5:9b` and
`gemma3:27b` through `ollama` 0.24.0 on 60 XL-Sum Turkish articles. The
sizing tables are computed exactly rather than simulated — the paired columns
sum McNemar's exact test over the joint distribution of the discordant cells —
after a simulated version of the paired table survived a full draft carrying a
column that cannot exist. The margin note in @sec-llm-eval-size says what
happened. Software: NumPy 2.5.2, `scipy` 1.18.1, `ollama` 0.24.0 on Python
3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- distinguish model benchmarks from *system* evaluation, and know which one
  you need;
- size an eval set from the difference you need to detect, rather than from
  what felt reasonable;
- audit an LLM judge before believing it, with controls that have known
  right answers;
- report results with uncertainty, and choose a paired design when it
  actually helps.

This is the chapter your statistics training was made for: applied LLM
evaluation is, at bottom, [measurement design under distribution
shift]{.hl}. Most of what follows is not new statistics. It is ordinary
statistics applied to a setting where almost nobody applies it.

## Benchmarks are not your evaluation {#sec-llm-eval-benchmarks}

A public benchmark answers *how does this model compare to other models on a
task someone else chose*. Your evaluation answers *does this system do my job
well enough to ship*. Those are different questions and the first one is only
occasionally evidence about the second.

Three specific reasons, in the order they will bite you.

**[Contamination](#gloss-benchmark-contamination){#term-benchmark-contamination .term-ref}.**
A benchmark published before a model was trained may be inside that model's
training data, and you cannot open the training set to find out
[@sainz2023nlp].

::: {#gloss-benchmark-contamination .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Benchmark contamination** — test items that were in a model's training data,
so its score can reflect memorisation rather than capability. You cannot inspect a
closed model's training set, but that does not make contamination
unmeasurable: @oren2024proving turns it into a hypothesis test you can run
through an API.
[↩](#term-benchmark-contamination){.term-back}
:::

This book
measured the effect on a smaller scale in @sec-sequence-labeling: **13.06% of
WikiANN's Turkish test set is byte-identical to a training sentence**, and the
score bonus that leakage produced fell monotonically with how much a system
memorises — +26.50 span F1 for a gazetteer, +16.25 for a CRF, +7.65 for a
fine-tuned encoder. Nobody had to be dishonest for that to happen.

Two things follow, and the second is why this is a section rather than a
warning. Contamination is **testable**, even on a model you cannot open:
@oren2024proving permutes a benchmark's item order and checks whether the
model gives higher likelihood to the canonical ordering, which is a real
hypothesis test you can run through an API — provided the API returns token
log-probabilities, which the test needs and not every closed API exposes. @sec-data-annotation and
@sec-pretraining both point at it; this is the chapter where you would run
it, before quoting a benchmark number you did not generate yourself. And the
structural answer since 2024 has been benchmarks that rotate their items
faster than models are trained — @white2025livebench replaces about a sixth
of its questions every month, trading comparability across time for a
contamination guarantee. Neither replaces your own eval set. Both make a
leaderboard number slightly less of a rumour.

**Saturation.** A benchmark is *saturated* when the best models score close
to its ceiling, so there is little room left for them to differ. When the headline models are at 88, 89 and 90, one point of
difference is competing with everything else that varies at that scale: the
benchmark's own label errors, its ambiguous items, and the prompt each lab
used. Close scores do not by themselves distinguish a small real difference
from measurement uncertainty — the models may genuinely differ by a point.
Assess the benchmark's uncertainty and its validity before reading anything into
the ranking.

**Construct mismatch.** The benchmark measures a task; you have a *system*,
which is a prompt, a retrieval step, a parser, a fallback, and a model. A
benchmark score cannot tell you that your JSON parser drops 2% of responses —
@sec-decoding measured a case where formatting failures were being counted as
reasoning failures, and enforcement moved accuracy from 70.7% to 88.0% with no
change to the model at all.

::: {.column-margin}
The useful role for public benchmarks is *screening*: they cheaply eliminate
models that are obviously unfit, and they tell you what is broadly possible.
Treat a leaderboard as a way to pick three candidates, never as a way to pick
one — and remember that a rank is a statistic with a sampling process behind
it. @singh2025leaderboard documents undisclosed private testing on the arena
that lets a provider evaluate many variants and publish only the best, 27 of
them before one release. Nobody has to cheat for a selection effect that size
to move a ranking. @liang2023holistic is worth reading for the opposite
reason: what it looks like when the sampling process is written down.
:::

**What we will look at.** First the sizing question, which has an exact answer
almost nobody computes and which turns out to disqualify the eval set most
teams already have. Then how to build one — where to sample from, why the
labelling order matters, and the harness bugs that report a plausible number
instead of crashing. Then an audit of an LLM judge against probes whose right
answers are known in advance, where the control everyone thinks to run is the
one that separates two judges least. And finally how to report a result
someone can act on, which is mostly a matter of never quoting a number without
also saying what it could not have detected.

## How big does your eval set need to be? {#sec-llm-eval-size}

Here is the question almost every LLM project answers by feel, and it has an
exact answer. Given a system that is right about 80% of the time, how large
must an eval set be to detect an improvement of *d* points, at 80%
[**statistical power**](#gloss-statistical-power){#term-statistical-power .term-ref}
and the conventional 5% significance level?

::: {#gloss-statistical-power .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Statistical power** — the probability that your evaluation detects a real
difference of a given size. An underpowered eval mostly produces *false
negatives* — a real improvement reported as "no difference" — and one more
subtle failure: among the comparisons that do clear significance, the effects
are systematically overstated, because only the luckily-large ones get there.
So low power costs you both the improvements you miss and the size of the ones
you find.
[↩](#term-statistical-power){.term-back}
:::

```text
smallest difference detectable at 80% power (two independent proportions,
baseline 80%, two-sided alpha = 0.05). The count is per system: 100 means
each of the two systems is scored on 100 items. Whether those are the same
100 items is the paired question, and the table below answers it.

     items      smallest detectable difference
        30            none — see below
        50                    17.5 points
       100                    13.4 points
       200                    10.0 points
       500                     6.6 points
     1,000                     4.8 points
     2,000                     3.4 points
```

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Size your own eval set</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof evalBase = Inputs.range([0.50, 0.95], {step: 0.01, value: 0.80,
  label: "current accuracy"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof evalDiff = Inputs.range([1, 20], {step: 1, value: 5,
  label: "difference you need to detect (points)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof evalPower = Inputs.radio(new Map([["80%", 0.80], ["90%", 0.90]]),
  {value: 0.80, label: "power"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Abramowitz–Stegun 26.2.23 inverse normal, good to ~4.5e-4 — plenty here
evalZ = p => {
  const t = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(p < 0.5 ? p : 1 - p));
  const x = t - (2.515517 + 0.802853 * t + 0.010328 * t * t) /
            (1 + 1.432788 * t + 0.189269 * t * t + 0.001308 * t * t * t);
  return p < 0.5 ? -x : x;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
evalN = {
  const d = evalDiff / 100, pa = evalBase, pb = Math.min(pa + d, 0.999);
  const za = evalZ(0.975), zb = evalZ(evalPower);
  const pbar = (pa + pb) / 2;
  const n = Math.pow(za * Math.sqrt(2 * pbar * (1 - pbar)) +
                     zb * Math.sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) + pb * (1 - pb)), 2) / (d * d);
  return Math.ceil(n);
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`To detect **${evalDiff} points** on top of ${(evalBase * 100).toFixed(0)}%
at ${(evalPower * 100).toFixed(0)}% power, you need about
**${evalN.toLocaleString()} items per system** — ${evalN > 500
  ? "more than most teams label, which is the useful thing to find out before running the comparison rather than after"
  : "a size you can realistically label"}.
A paired design needs fewer *if* the two systems mostly agree, and fewer still
the more they agree; see the table below.${evalBase + evalDiff / 100 > 0.97
  ? " **Above about 97% this number stops being trustworthy**, because the normal approximation's variance term collapses as the target approaches 1.00. Use an exact test — `scipy.stats.fisher_exact` or `binomtest` — anywhere in that range."
  : ""}`
```
:::

[At thirty items there is no answer, because no difference is large enough.]{.hl}
Against a system that is right 80% of the time, even a *perfect* replacement —
one that is right 100% of the time — reaches only **57%** power on thirty
items. That figure is from an exact test, and the exact test is the one to
quote here: the normal approximation everywhere else in this section returns
75%, but at *p* = 1.00 its variance term is exactly zero and there is nothing
left for it to approximate. Both exact routes agree — Fisher's exact test with
thirty items per arm and McNemar's exact test on thirty paired items both give
0.5725. A hundred items per system detects 13.4 points. Most real improvements
are two to five.

That is worth sitting with, because thirty items is a common size; it is the
size this chapter's own exercise asked for in an earlier draft.

This does **not** mean small eval sets are useless. It means they answer a
different question, and the distinction is the most practically useful thing
in this chapter:

| eval set size | what it is genuinely for |
|:--|:--|
| **20–50 items** | finding *failure modes*. Read every output by hand. You are looking for categories of wrongness, not for a number, and thirty items surfaces them well — this is a real job, and the size is right for it |
| **100–300 items** | catching *large* regressions — a broken parser, a prompt that stopped working, a model swap that went badly |
| **500+ items** | comparing two systems that are actually close, which is the case whenever you are tuning rather than fixing |

: Three different jobs, three different sizes {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

The failure to distinguish these is why so much prompt engineering is
folklore. Thirty examples were tried, one prompt looked better, and the
difference was smaller than the noise floor by an order of magnitude.

### What pairing buys, and when it does not

@sec-prompting used McNemar's test [@mcnemar1947note] on a 14.67-point spread
that overlapping confidence intervals would have called inconclusive — raw
$p = 0.0009$, and 0.062 after correcting for the 66 pairs the extreme one was
picked from. The
comparison there was **paired** — the same 150 reviews through every prompt —
and pairing is the standard advice.

The advice is right and it is not unconditional, because McNemar's test throws
away every item the two systems agree on. It looks only at the items where
exactly one of the two systems is right, and asks whether those split 50/50
between them, as they would if neither system were better. So what pairing buys depends on how
often they disagree, which is an empirical property of *your* systems:

```text
power to detect a 5-point difference: 80% baseline against 85%,
two-sided alpha = 0.05

            unpaired,     McNemar on n paired items, by how often
   items    n per arm     the two systems disagree
            (2n items)      10%      20%      30%      35%
       30       0.07        0.01     0.03     0.04     0.04
       50       0.10        0.06     0.07     0.06     0.06
      100       0.15        0.24     0.14     0.11     0.10
      200       0.26        0.54     0.30     0.21     0.19
      500       0.55        0.94     0.68     0.50     0.44
    1,000       0.84        1.00     0.94     0.81     0.75

The table stops at 35% because two systems at 80% and 85% cannot disagree
more than that: delta_max = 2(1 - p_B) + (p_B - p_A) = 0.35. Past it the
"both wrong" cell of the 2x2 table would have to hold a negative
probability. Note the item counts: the unpaired column is a study with n
items in each arm, so 2n items in total, while the paired columns run the
same n items through both systems. Note also the tests: the unpaired column
is the normal-approximation z-test, the paired columns are exact McNemar.
Fisher's exact test on the unpaired side would give 0.04, 0.06, 0.11, 0.22
and 0.52 for the first five rows.
```

**Pairing pays more the more the two systems agree, and the
threshold is one you can compute.** Write $\Delta = p_B - p_A$ for the true
accuracy difference, $\bar{p} = (p_A + p_B)/2$ for the average accuracy and
$\bar{q} = 1 - \bar{p}$. McNemar's asymptotic statistic is roughly
$\sqrt{n}\,\Delta/\sqrt{\delta}$, where $\delta$ is the disagreement rate;
the two-arm unpaired statistic is roughly $\sqrt{n}\,\Delta/\sqrt{2\bar{p}\bar{q}}$.
So pairing wins, to this approximation, when $\delta < 2\bar{p}\bar{q}$, which for an 80%
system against an 85% one is **28.9%** — and it wins while using half the
items. That number is not arbitrary either: it is almost exactly the disagreement rate two
*independent* systems would show,
$p_A(1-p_B) + (1-p_A)p_B = 0.80 \times 0.15 + 0.20 \times 0.85 = 0.29$ (the
two differ by $\Delta^2/2$, here 0.00125). Below
it your systems are positively correlated and pairing exploits the
correlation. Above it they are anti-correlated, which is rare between two
versions of the same system.

Read the table row by row and the practical rule falls out. At 10%
disagreement, 200 paired items reach 0.54 where 200 items in each of two arms
— twice the labelling — reach 0.26. At 30% the paired design on n items has
fallen behind the unpaired design on 2n items. So: comparing two prompts, two checkpoints, or two decoding settings —
cases where the systems agree on most items — pair, and get the answer on half
the labelling. Comparing two genuinely different architectures that disagree
constantly, pairing buys little and the honest move is a bigger eval set
rather than a cleverer test.

What does **not** happen is pairing costing you anything on data you already
have. An LLM eval is paired *whenever you run both systems on the same items*.
That is the normal design, but check it rather than assume it: a
comparison against a number from someone else's run, or against a different
sample, is not paired and cannot be analysed as if it were. When the items
*are* shared, analysing them as two independent samples looks more
powerful past the independence point, but only because the test no longer has
the error rate it claims. Computed exactly at n = 500 under a true null of 80%
against 80%, where independence sits at 32% disagreement, the unpaired
analysis rejects 0.05% of the time at 10% disagreement, 5.0% at 32%, and
**6.4%** at 36% — it buys the extra power with false positives. McNemar's
exact test stays between 3.7% and 4.2% across the same range, conservative in
the way an exact test on a discrete statistic is. On a fixed eval set the
paired test is never the wrong choice. It is only sometimes not much of a
gain.

::: {.anlp-widget}


```{ojs}
of two arms**, so 1,000. They cross close to the independence point, which is the
whole content of the rule — a little before it, at about 27%, because the
paired curve is the slightly conservative exact McNemar test while the flat
line is the normal approximation. Put Fisher's exact test on the unpaired side
(0.52 at 500 per arm) and the crossing moves onto 28.9%. The shaded band is the stretch of axis I published
a column in — at 80% against 85% the two systems cannot disagree on more than
35% of items, and a plot makes that obvious in a way six columns of numbers
did not.`
```

:::

::: {.column-margin}
I got this backwards twice. First I fixed the disagreement rate at
@sec-prompting's 30.7%, found that pairing bought nothing, and briefly believed
I had refuted a textbook result. What I had actually found is that 30.7% sits
just above 28.9%, the rate two independent systems at these accuracies would
show, so there was no correlation left to exploit — a fact about the input I
chose, not about McNemar. And it was the wrong input. 30.7% is the share of
reviews on which the twelve variants did not all agree, not how often two
prompts disagree: two variants disagreed on a median of 12% of reviews and at
most 28.7%, and the best and worst prompts on 42 of 150 (28.0%). Then, fixing it, I ran the simulation out to 40%
disagreement and published a column that cannot exist at these marginals. The
closed-form check in the script caught neither, because it only ever covered
the unpaired side. The table above is now computed exactly, and the general
lesson is cheap: when a paired design stops helping, compute
$p_A(1-p_B) + (1-p_A)p_B$ and see whether you have simply reached
independence.
:::

## Building an eval set {#sec-llm-eval-building}

An eval set is a **sample**, and everything your statistics training says
about samples applies. Three decisions do almost all the work.

**Sample from real traffic, not from imagination.** Invented test cases are
systematically cleaner, better spelled, and more typical than what users send.
If you have no traffic yet, use whatever is closest — support tickets, search
logs, a colleague's real questions — and label the gap explicitly. A hundred
real items beat a thousand invented ones, and this is the single highest-value
decision in the chapter.

**Stratify deliberately, then say what you did.** Real traffic is dominated by
easy cases, so a uniform sample spends most of its items confirming that the
easy cases still work. Oversample the hard slices, the rare-but-costly
categories, and the languages you actually serve — and then, when you report a
headline number, either reweight to the traffic distribution or say plainly
that the number is on a stratified sample. Both are fine; silence is not.

**Include the cases with no good answer.** Questions your system should refuse,
inputs that are out of scope, documents that do not contain the answer.
@sec-rag found this to be the test nobody runs, and @sec-multimodal found a
model that refused 90 times out of 90 when asked for something absent — a
result you only learn by asking.

### Label the data before you look at model output

The order matters more than it sounds. Labels written after seeing a system's
answers drift toward those answers, and the drift is invisible afterwards.
Write the rubric, label a sample against it, measure how often two labellers
agree, and *then* run anything. Report that agreement as Cohen's $\kappa$
[@cohen1960coefficient] rather than as a raw percentage, because a raw
percentage includes the agreement two people would reach without reading the
items: on an eval set where both labellers call 80% of items "correct", two
labellers assigning those rates independently already agree 68% of the time
($0.8^2 + 0.2^2$), so a raw 70% is $\kappa \approx 0.06$ — essentially no
agreement beyond that baseline. Report the confusion table beside it, because
on a heavily skewed set kappa is low and unstable even for careful labellers
(@sec-data-annotation shows both effects). For more than two labellers, or an ordinal rubric, use
Krippendorff's $\alpha$ [@krippendorff2018content]. Human agreement is not a
hard ceiling on system scores — measured against a reconciled gold standard a
system can beat any single labeller — but a system scoring far above the
labellers is usually fitting their shared quirks rather than the task.
@sec-data-annotation has the rest of the machinery.

### Version the eval like code

The eval set is a dependency of every number you report, so it belongs in the
repository, in a file, under review, with a changelog. Two rules that pay for
themselves:

- **Never edit an item in place.** Add a new one and retire the old, so a
  score from March remains comparable to a score from June, and a score that
  moved because the *test* changed is distinguishable from one that moved
  because the system did.
- **Keep a held-out slice you look at rarely.** An eval set you tune against
  every day is a training set. @sec-classification's split discipline is the
  same discipline, one level up.

### The harness bugs that produce good numbers

A broken evaluation harness usually does not crash. It reports something
plausible, and there is an asymmetry that makes this dangerous: **a bad number
gets investigated, a good one gets published.** Two bugs from this book's own
work, both caught late:

- A reasoning model was given a 24-token generation budget. `ollama` returns
  chain-of-thought in a separate `thinking` field, so the whole budget went
  there, the answer field stayed empty, every response failed to parse, and
  each failure fell through to a majority-class default. The run reported
  **93.75% accuracy** — which was exactly the majority baseline.
- A tuned threshold was applied to the wrong side of a probability, scoring a
  model at 51.50 macro-F1 instead of 80.23.

Neither raised an error. The guards that would have caught them are cheap:
**log the parse rate per run and abort below 50%**, smoke-test every
model×condition on two dozen items before an overnight queue, and quote
*median* seconds per item rather than the mean — machine stalls in this book's
own runs made one mean nine times its median.

## LLM-as-judge, audited {#sec-llm-eval-judge}

Those guards catch a harness that lies to you. They do not catch an
*instrument* that lies to you — and the most common instrument in 2026 is
another model.

Using a model to grade another model's output is now the default for anything
that cannot be scored with an exact match. It is a reasonable idea and it is
also **a measuring instrument you did not calibrate**. So calibrate it — with
probes whose right answer you already know, which means you can score the
judge rather than trust it.

Four probes, on 60 Turkish news articles, comparing summaries. The
"professional summary" below is the one-sentence summary XL-Sum ships with each
article, written by BBC Türkçe's journalists — the dataset's reference summary
(@sec-summarization). Three of the
probes were run for this chapter:

1. **Identical.** A and B are the same text. The only correct verdict is a
   tie. This is @sec-summarization's copied-text control, moved from metrics
   to preferences.
2. **Position.** A real comparison — the professional summary against the
   article's first sentence — run in **both orders**. A judge without
   [**position bias**](#gloss-position-bias){#term-position-bias .term-ref}
   [@wang2024large] returns the same winner both times.

3. **Verbosity.** The same summary, padded with contentless filler. No
   information is added, so preferring the padded version is preferring
   length.
4. **Self-preference.** Have each candidate model summarise the same 60
   articles, then ask each judge to compare its own family's output against
   the other's, in both orders. A judge with no self-preference splits 50/50
   once the orders are averaged. **This is the probe I did not run**, and it
   is the one that matters most when the judge and the system come from the
   same lab: @panickssery2024llm found the strength of the bias tracks how
   well a model recognises its own writing, which suggests it may grow, not
   shrink, as models get better at recognising themselves. The setup here —
   two models, both able to summarise — could run it in an afternoon.

::: {#gloss-position-bias .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Position bias** — a judge preferring the candidate in a particular slot
(first or second, depending on the model) regardless of content.
Measured directly by running the same comparison in both orders and counting
how often the verdict flips. [↩](#term-position-bias){.term-back}
:::

```text
                                      n     qwen3.5:9b     gemma3:27b   Fisher p

 1. identical texts → called a tie    60       100.0%         100.0%          —
                                           [94.0, 100]    [94.0, 100]

 2. same winner in both orders        60        61.7%          85.0%    0.00674
                                          [49.0, 72.9]   [73.9, 91.9]
    picked whichever was in slot A   60x2       57.5%          54.2%          —
    preferred the professional
    summary, both orders pooled      60x2       51.7%          74.2%    0.00048
                                          [42.8, 60.4]   [65.7, 81.2]

 3. preferred the padded copy         60        28.3%           0.0%    <0.0001
                                          [18.5, 40.8]     [0.0, 6.0]

Intervals are Wilson at 95%. The rows marked 60x2 pool two judgments per
article -- the same comparison in both orders -- and those two judgments are
not independent observations, so the intervals printed for them are narrower
than they should be. Computed on the 60 articles instead, the 51.7% becomes
[39.3, 63.8] -- itself approximate, since a per-article score of 0, 1/2 or 1 is
not a Bernoulli trial. The Fisher column treats the two judges as independent
samples, which they are not: both read the same 60 articles.
```

### Both judges pass the test everyone runs

The identical-text control is the sanity check a careful team would think to
run, and **both models score 100%**. Sixty pairs of byte-identical text, sixty
ties, no exceptions. Even that deserves an interval, by this chapter's own
rule: 60/60 has a Wilson interval (a confidence interval for a proportion
that stays sensible at small $n$ and at 0% or 100%) of [94.0, 100], so the
probe is also consistent with a judge that misses as many as one comparison
in seventeen. It is a
floor test, not a certificate. And if it were your whole audit you would
conclude you have two sound judges and pick on price.

Then the probes that discriminate:

[The small judge changes its answer on 38% of items when you swap the
order.]{.hl} Same two texts, same question, different verdict. That is not a
hard-comparison problem — it is a property of the instrument, and it means
more than a third of its verdicts carry no information about the summaries at
all.

It also **preferred the professional summary only 51.7% of the time** over the
article's opening sentence. Read that as a preference rate rather than an
accuracy: calling 50% "chance" presumes the professional summary is the correct
answer, and no human judgement in this run establishes that. The interval is [42.8, 60.4]
if you count all 120 judgments and [39.3, 63.8] if you count the 60 articles,
and neither is quite right: the two orders of one article are not two
independent facts, and averaging them into a 0, ½ or 1 per article does not make
a Bernoulli trial either. An article-level bootstrap is the honest interval, and
this run did not keep what it needs. Every version of the interval
comfortably contains 50, which is the only thing the conclusion needs.

In fairness to the model, the comparison is not trivial: an article's opening
sentence is fluent, on-topic text written by the same journalist. But it is not
a strong summary on this corpus — @sec-summarization found lead bias weak here,
with the first sentence scoring 12.75 ROUGE-1 against 24.89 for the best single
sentence, and being the closest match to the reference only 15.8% of the time.
So ROUGE, at least, does not rate the two as close. Until a human rubric says which of the two should
win, a judge whose preference between them is indistinguishable from a coin has
not shown that it can rank your system's outputs either.

The larger judge looks better on every probe: 85.0% order-consistency, a 74.2%
preference for the professional summary, and it never once fell for the
padding. How firmly each gap stands is less settled than the p-value column
suggests, because those p-values come from the wrong test — see the next
paragraph — and the margins alone cannot supply the right one. The padded-copy
gap is safe under any pairing: the larger judge never preferred the padding, so
all 17 disagreements run one way and exact McNemar gives
$p = 2 \times 2^{-17} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-5}$. The order-consistency gap is
not: 37/60 against 51/60 is consistent with anything from 14 disagreements all
one way ($p = 0.00012$) to 23 against 9 ($p = 0.020$, or 0.060 after Bonferroni
over three tests). This chapter therefore does not claim that all three gaps
survive correction. And say how many tests you ran even when it seems to change
nothing: five comparisons at $\alpha = 0.05$ flag something about a quarter of
the time, if they are independent, on a run where nothing differs.

**What the p-values in that table assume, and should not.** Fisher's exact
test compares two *independent* samples. These two judges read the same 60
articles, so the comparison is paired and the right test is McNemar's — the
test this chapter spends a whole section recommending. Running it needs the
item-level agreement between the two judges, and this run stored only the
margins, so it is the first thing to add. The direction of the correction is
not obvious either: pairing normally sharpens a comparison of correlated
raters, while the two pooled rows count each article twice and that works the
other way. What survives without the item-level table is the ordering and the
padding result; what does not survive is the precision of the two smaller
p-values.

::: {.column-margin}
A rough internal check on @sec-llm-eval-size: the sizing table says 50 items
per system detects 17.5 points, and the gap here **on order-consistency** is
23.3 points — 85.0 against 61.7 — over 60 articles. Rough because the table's
rows are unpaired and per-arm while this comparison is 60 articles read by
both judges, so the two are not the same design. The conclusion survives that
sloppiness in either direction: the experiment was adequately powered *for the
difference it found*, and would have been badly underpowered for a 5-point
one, which is worth remembering before reading anything into the slot-A
numbers (57.5% against 54.2%), where the design has no power at all.
:::

The control a careful team thinks to run is the flat one: both judges land on

::::

### Verbosity bias did not reproduce

Judges have been measured preferring longer answers [@zheng2023judging].
Neither of these did: `qwen3.5:9b` preferred the padded copy 28.3% of the time
[18.5, 40.8] and `gemma3:27b` never — 0/60, which is a Wilson interval of
[0.0, 6.0], so the claim available from that cell is that its rate of falling
for obvious padding is under about one in sixteen, not that it is zero. I will
state the rest narrowly too, the way @sec-rag's needle result had to be
stated: my filler was **obviously** contentless boilerplate — three sentences
of "the situation is as described above" — and detecting that is a much easier
task than resisting a genuinely more detailed, better-organised, longer
answer.

"Did not reproduce" means neither judge *preferred* the longer copy on
balance (in more than half the cases). It does
not mean `qwen3.5:9b` handled the probe well: choosing a strictly worse copy
more than one time in four is still an error rate, just not a length bias.
What I measured is that both judges mostly reject obvious padding. What I did not
measure is what they do with elaboration that adds real structure but no
correctness, which is the case the folklore is actually about.

### What to do about it

Five changes, and the first has to happen before you collect any numbers rather
than after.

- **Run the probes before you run the eval.** The three that ran here take an
  afternoon between them, the fourth about the same, and they change which
  judge you use.
- **Randomise or average over order.** Present each pair in both orders and
  count only the items where the verdict agrees, or randomise and accept the
  extra variance. If you drop the items that flip, report how many are left: a
  verdict that changes with order is an abstention, and the coverage rule below
  applies to it. Reporting a single-order pairwise result from a judge with a
  38% flip rate is reporting the coin, not the systems.
- **Prefer pairwise over absolute scoring**, but know what it costs. Asking
  "which is better" is more reliable than asking for a 1–5 rating, because a
  rating scale drifts between calls and has no anchor — @liu2023geval is the
  careful version of the absolute-scoring approach if you need one. The first
  cost is that pairwise is exactly where position bias lives — an absolute
  score of one answer has no slot A — so pairwise only pays if you also follow
  the both-orders rule above. The second
  is that pairwise comparisons do not aggregate into a score without more
  structure, and the structure has a name: a **Bradley–Terry** model
  [@bradley1952rank], which fits one latent strength per system from the win
  matrix and is what an Elo leaderboard is doing underneath. If you need an
  absolute number rather than an ordering, the alternative worth trying is a
  *rubric* — an item-specific checklist scored yes/no, which gives the anchor
  a 1–5 scale lacks while still adding up.
- **Calibrate against human labels on a subsample.** Fifty items labelled by
  hand tells you the judge's agreement rate with the thing you actually care
  about — as $\kappa$, like the labellers' agreement. Read it against the
  human–human $\kappa$: a judge that agrees with you about as well as a second
  person does is as good as a second labeller, and one far below that is not.
  Without that number, a judge score is a measurement in unknown units.
- **Never let the judge be the same model as the system under test**
  [@panickssery2024llm], or at least never without running the fourth probe
  above and measuring the self-preference that setup invites.

## Reporting a result someone can act on {#sec-llm-eval-reporting}

Report uncertainty next to every point estimate, so a reader can judge how much
the result actually supports. Five rules, all cheap:

**Report an interval, and say how you got it.** For a proportion, Wilson
[@wilson1927probable] beats the textbook normal approximation at the small
sample sizes this field actually uses — it does not produce impossible bounds
below 0 or above 1. Every percentage in this chapter carries one. For anything
that is *not* a proportion — a ROUGE mean, an average 1–5 rating, cost per
item — resample the items instead:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import bootstrap
res = bootstrap((scores,), np.mean, confidence_level=0.95,
                n_resamples=10_000, method="BCa", rng=0)
print(res.confidence_interval)
```

And resample at the level the data is clustered at, not the level it is stored
at. The judge probes above produce two judgments per article; resampling 120
judgments understates the interval, and resampling 60 articles does not.
@miller2024error works through the general case — cluster-robust standard
errors, paired differences, and the planning arithmetic of
@sec-llm-eval-size — and is the single most useful reference on this page.

**Use the paired test when the systems mostly agree**, per
@sec-llm-eval-size, and say which you used. Two overlapping marginal intervals
are not evidence of no difference: @sec-prompting's 14.67-point spread had
overlapping intervals and McNemar found p = 0.0009 — 0.062 once corrected for
the 66 pairs it was picked from, so pairing sharpened the evidence without
settling it.

**Quote the median for latency, and the tail — not the mean alone.** One
stalled request rewrites a mean. This book's own timing runs produced a mean
nine times its median, and a concurrent job made one configuration look
nineteen times slower than an identical one, which is why no chapter here
publishes a latency number collected while something else was running. The
median plus p95 and p99 is what describes the user experience. Keep the mean
where it is the right statistic — expected cost per request and capacity
planning are both sums, and a sum is a mean times a count — but never let it
stand in for the typical case.

**Report coverage alongside accuracy whenever anything can abstain, fail to
parse, or time out.** An accuracy computed only over successful responses is
not an accuracy — @sec-decoding's abstention result moved 86.75% to 92.50%
purely by declining the hardest fifth, which is an improvement only if you
also say you answered 80% of the questions.

**Say how many comparisons you made.** One headline number needs no
correction, provided it was not itself picked from many. Twelve slices at
$\alpha = 0.05$ on a run where nothing changed flag **0.6 of them on average**
and, if the twelve tests are independent, flag **at least one 46% of the time**
($1 - 0.95^{12}$); slices that overlap change the second figure. Two different
statements, and the second is the one that
matters when you are staring at a single report. A regression report is usually
twelve slices.
Holm's step-down correction —
`statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests(p, method="holm")` — is never less
powerful than Bonferroni and, like it, does not need the tests to be
independent. The judge table above
reports three tests, and what survives correction is the shorter list given
under that table rather than the p-value column; saying which is the whole of
the discipline.

### Regression testing, which is the point of all this

The eval set earns its keep when a change lands. Run it on every prompt
change, model version, and dependency bump, and store the per-item results
rather than the summary — because the useful question after a drop is *which
items changed*, and a stored aggregate cannot answer it.

Two thresholds worth agreeing in advance, before anyone has a stake in the
answer: the size of drop that blocks a release, and the size that merely opens
an investigation. Set them from @sec-llm-eval-size's table rather than from a
round number, because a rule that blocks on a 2-point drop in a 100-item eval
will fire constantly on noise and then be ignored, which is worse than having
no rule.

There is a second reason a threshold fires on noise, and it is not sample
size. Running the same test on every merge is repeated significance testing:
if each run draws fresh randomness — a new sample of items, or sampled
generations — a pipeline that changed nothing still trips a 5% alarm about once
in twenty runs, and with better than even odds within fourteen
($1 - 0.95^{14} = 0.51$). Re-scoring the same deterministic outputs on the same
fixed set is not a new chance to fail; it gives the same answer every time. Two cheap
fixes. Set the alarm from the eval's own noise level: on a 100-item eval at
80%, a swing of about 11 points happens by chance one run in twenty, and a real
drop has to be about 13 points before the eval catches it reliably, so a rule
below that range fires on noise. And treat the alarm as a trigger
for a second, larger run rather than as a verdict. If what you actually want
is a threshold you can watch continuously as items accumulate, the tool is an
always-valid sequential test [@johari2022always] — a fixed-$\alpha$ test
looked at repeatedly no longer has the $\alpha$ it claims.

## Intuition checks {#sec-llm-eval-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. All six are questions this chapter settled
with a measurement rather than an argument.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your model scores 91 on a public benchmark. What have you learned?

That it is not obviously unfit, and little else. You have not learned whether
the benchmark was in its training data — @sec-sequence-labeling found **13.06%
of one benchmark's test set duplicated in its own training split** — nor
whether the benchmark is saturated, nor whether it measures your task.
Benchmarks are a screen for picking three candidates. Your eval decides
between them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Is a 30-item eval set worth building?

Yes, for the right question — but not for comparing systems. At thirty items
there is **no** difference detectable at 80% power against an 80%-accurate
baseline: even a replacement that is right every single time reaches only
**57%**, on an exact test. (The normal approximation says 75% and should not
be believed at *p* = 1.00, where its variance term is zero.)
What thirty items is excellent at is *finding failure modes*: read all thirty outputs by hand and
you will find categories of wrongness that no aggregate score would surface.
Use small sets to learn what breaks, large sets to decide what ships.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Should you always use a paired test?

Yes, on data you already have — but know what it buys. McNemar discards every
item the systems agree on, so its *gain* depends on the disagreement rate, and
the threshold is computable: pairing on n items beats an unpaired study with n
in each arm roughly when the disagreement rate is below
$2\bar{p}\bar{q}$, which for 80% against 85% is **28.9%** — almost exactly
the rate two independent systems would show. Comparing two prompts, which agree on most
items, pairing wins on half the labelling. Comparing two very different
systems it buys little, and a bigger eval set is the honest fix. What it never
does is cost you power: the unpaired analysis of paired data only looks
stronger above the independence point because its false-positive rate has
drifted to about 6%.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your LLM judge gives two identical texts a tie every time. Is it reliable?

You have learned that it passes the easiest possible check, and nothing more.
Both judges here scored **100%** on that probe and then diverged sharply: one
flipped its verdict on 38% of items when the order was swapped and preferred
the professional summary 51.7% of the time; the other flipped on 15% and
preferred it 74.2% of the time. Those are preference rates, not accuracies —
which summary *should* win is a question for a human rubric. The
control everyone runs is the one that discriminates least.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Two prompts score 84% and 79% on your 100-item eval. Is the first better?

You cannot tell from those numbers. A 100-item eval detects about **13 points**
at 80% power, and this is 5. Pairing does not rescue it. If the same 100
items went through both prompts, McNemar's exact test on the disagreements is
the right test, but a 5-item gap is at best 5 disagreements against 0, which
gives a two-sided $p = 2 \times 0.5^5 = 0.0625$; more disagreements in both
directions only raise it. Paired or not, the honest report is "no detectable
difference at this sample size", which is a different statement from "no
difference".
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your eval harness reports 93.75% accuracy. What do you check first?

The parse rate. That exact number came from a run where a reasoning model
spent its whole token budget in a `thinking` field, every answer failed to
parse, and each failure defaulted to the majority class — so the harness was
reporting the **majority baseline** as a result. A bad number gets
investigated and a good one gets published, so a suspiciously good number
deserves the same scrutiny a bad one gets automatically.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-llm-eval-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the measurement

**Q: How would you evaluate an LLM feature?**

Start by separating the two questions — is the model capable, and does my
system work — and say that public benchmarks answer only the first. Then give
the structure: a versioned eval set sampled from real traffic, sized from the
difference you need to detect, including cases the system should refuse, with
human labels collected before any model output is seen. Finish on reporting:
intervals, paired tests where the systems mostly agree, and coverage alongside
accuracy.

**Q: Your eval set has 100 items and the new prompt scores 5 points higher.
Ship it?**

Not on that evidence. A hundred items detects about 13 points at 80% power, so
5 points is inside the noise. Pairing helps less than people expect here:
McNemar on the disagreements can find effects the marginal intervals cannot,
but not this one — a 5-item gap is at best 5 disagreements against 0, and the
exact two-sided p is then 0.0625. The answer that shows judgement is naming what you would do next:
either enlarge the eval, or ship it as a low-risk change while explicitly not
claiming an improvement.

**Q: What is wrong with using GPT-4-class models as judges?**

Nothing, provided you calibrate one first. The failure is treating it as an
oracle rather than an instrument. Name the specific biases and how you would
measure each: position, by running both orders — measured here at a 38% flip
rate for a small judge and 15% for a large one; verbosity, by padding an
answer without adding information; self-preference, by never letting the judge
grade its own family without checking. And calibrate against human labels on a
subsample, because otherwise the score has no units.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: How do you catch a broken evaluation?**

With controls that have known answers, because a broken harness usually
returns something plausible rather than crashing. Score a reference against
itself and require a perfect result. Log the parse rate and abort below a
threshold. Compare against a majority-class baseline every run — if your model
matches it exactly, that is usually a bug: inspect the harness and the
model's raw outputs at once. And say the thing
that makes all of it necessary: a bad number gets investigated, a good one
gets published.

**Q: Your production quality dropped and the eval did not move. What
happened?**

Most likely the eval no longer resembles traffic — inputs drifted, a new
customer segment arrived, or the eval was built from imagined cases in the
first place. Check the input distribution before touching the model. The
second candidate is that the failure is in a part of the system the eval does
not exercise: a parser, a retrieval step, a timeout. That is why per-item
results are stored rather than aggregates, and why coverage is reported
alongside accuracy.

## Lab: audit a judge, then size your eval {#sec-llm-eval-lab}

Do the audit before the eval, in that order, because a judge you have not
scored turns every number that follows into a measurement in unknown units.

### Step 1 — write 50 items from real traffic

Real inputs, and include five your system should refuse. Label them yourself
before running anything.

### Step 2 — measure human agreement

Have a second person label 25 of them, then compute **Cohen's $\kappa$**
(`sklearn.metrics.cohen_kappa_score`) as well as raw agreement, because raw
agreement on a skewed eval set is mostly the agreement two labellers would
reach without reading the items. Treat 0.4 as a rough warning line, not a
verdict: at 25 items the interval around kappa is wide, and on a skewed set
kappa is low even for careful labellers (@sec-data-annotation). A low kappa
*with* a confusion table full of genuine disagreements says the rubric is the
problem, not the system — fix it before building an eval on it.

### Step 3 — run the identical-text probe

Ask your judge to compare an output with itself, 30 times. If it does not call
a tie, stop and fix the prompt before doing anything else.

### Step 4 — run the position probe

Take 30 real comparisons and run each in both orders. Report the flip rate
**with a Wilson interval**, because at 30 pairs the interval is wide — an
observed 6/30 spans [9.5, 37.3] — and a bare 20% threshold would be deciding
on noise. Treat this step as a screen rather than a measurement: if the
interval's *lower* bound clears 10%, you have a judge whose single-order
verdicts are partly coin flips and you should be averaging over orders. If you
need the flip rate itself to within a few points, @sec-llm-eval-size's table
says what that costs.

### Step 5 — calibrate against your own labels

On the 50 labelled items, how often does the judge agree with you — again as
$\kappa$, not as a raw percentage? That is the number that converts judge
scores into something meaningful. Put it next to the human–human $\kappa$
from Step 2: the judge is good enough when it agrees with you about as well
as your second labeller did.

### Step 6 — size the next eval

Decide the smallest difference that would change a decision. Use
@sec-llm-eval-size's table to find the item count it requires. If the count is
larger than you can label, say so explicitly rather than shipping an
underpowered comparison and calling it a result.

### What to hand in

The two probe results, the judge–human agreement rate, the human–human
agreement rate, and one sentence naming the smallest difference your eval set
can actually detect.

## Exercises {#sec-llm-eval-exercises}

1. **Size your current eval.** Take an eval set you already use, find its item
   count in @sec-llm-eval-size's table, and write down the smallest difference
   it can detect. Compare that to the differences you have been reporting.
2. **Audit your judge.** Run the identical-text and position probes on
   whatever judge you use now. Report the tie rate and the flip rate.
3. **Both orders.** Take a pairwise evaluation you have already run and rerun
   it with the order swapped. How many verdicts change? What does that do to
   your conclusion?
4. **Find the agreement ceiling.** Have two people label the same 30 items
   independently. Compute Cohen's $\kappa$ as well as raw agreement, and note
   how far apart they are. Compare both to the accuracy you have been
   reporting for your system.
5. **Build the absence slice.** Add ten items your system should refuse.
   Measure how often it does. This is usually the fastest way to find a real
   problem.
6. **Break your own harness.** Set a generation budget too small for a
   reasoning model and see what your pipeline reports. Then add the parse-rate
   guard that would have caught it.
7. **Power in reverse.** Pick the smallest improvement that would change a
   decision at your organisation. Compute the eval size it needs. If you
   cannot afford it, write down what you will do instead — that sentence is a
   more useful deliverable than most eval reports.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-llm-eval-deeper}

Before reading anything: count the items in your current eval set and look up
the smallest difference it can detect. If you have been reporting differences
below that, everything else here is urgent.

## What to remember {#sec-llm-eval-summary}

- **A public benchmark screens; your eval decides.** Contamination is real —
  @sec-sequence-labeling found **13.06%** of one benchmark's test set
  duplicated in its training split — and it is testable rather than merely
  suspectable, even on a closed model [@oren2024proving]. On a saturated
  leaderboard, close scores cannot by themselves separate a real difference
  from measurement noise, and a leaderboard
  *rank* is a statistic with a sampling process behind it
  [@singh2025leaderboard].
- **Size the eval from the difference you need to detect.** On a system that
  is right 80% of the time, **30 items do not reach 80% power even for a
  perfect replacement** — it reaches 57% on an exact test — 100
  items per system detects 13.4 points, and 1,000 detects 4.8. Most real
  improvements are 2–5 points, so most eval sets in use cannot see the thing
  they were built to see.
- **Small eval sets are for finding failure modes, not for comparing
  systems.** Twenty to fifty items read by hand will tell you *what* breaks.
  Telling you *which is better* takes hundreds of items for the 2–5-point
  differences most changes produce — how many depends on the effect size and on
  whether the design is paired.
- **Pairing helps more the more the systems agree.** At 10%
  disagreement, 200 paired items reach 0.54 power against 0.26 for 200 items
  in each of two arms — twice the power on half the labelling. The gain shrinks
  to nothing at about **28.9% disagreement**, which is essentially where two
  systems would be statistically independent, and it never goes negative on data you already
  have.
- **Audit the judge with controls that have known answers.** Both judges here
  scored **100%** on identical-text ties — 60/60, which is still only
  [94.0, 100] — and then one flipped its verdict on **38% of items** when the
  order was swapped and preferred the professional summary 51.7% of the time,
  while the other flipped on 15% and preferred it 74.2% — preference rates,
  not accuracies. The control everyone runs is the
  one that discriminates least.
- **Run pairwise comparisons in both orders**, count only the items where the
  two agree, and report how many items that leaves. A single-order result from a judge with a 38% flip rate is
  reporting the coin.
- **Verbosity bias did not reproduce here** — `qwen3.5:9b` picked the
  obviously padded copy 28.3% of the time and `gemma3:27b` never, so neither
  favoured it — but that is a narrow claim about obvious padding,
  not about the elaborate-but-empty answers the folklore is really about.
- **A bad number gets investigated; a good one gets published.** That
  asymmetry, not the bug, is what to design against. Log parse rates, keep a
  majority-class baseline in every run, score a reference against itself, and
  treat a suspiciously good result with the suspicion a bad one gets for free.
